high.title: Deep link loads an attacker URL into an authenticated WebView
high.description:
4 findings in this app combine into one exploitable path: "WebView loads a URL taken from an Intent extra", "WebView sends HTTP auth credentials to any host", "WebView loading outside URLs shares the app's cookies" and "WebView has JavaScript enabled".

Attack path:
1. Attacker sends Intent to WebActivity with a crafted 'ssn' extra
2. WebActivity loads the attacker-controlled URL into the WebView
3. The attacker's server requests HTTP authentication
4. The WebView triggers MyWebViewClient.onReceivedHttpAuthRequest
5. MyWebViewClient sends the app's credentials to the attacker's host
high.impact: The deep link's URL parameter reaches the WebView without a host allowlist, so an attacker picks the page that renders inside the app's trusted UI while it still holds the user's session. Depending on the WebView's settings that means cookie and token theft, local file reads through file://, or script execution via javascript: and data: URLs.
high.recommendation: Parse the incoming URL and compare its host against an exact allowlist. Reject every scheme except https. Do not rely on contains() or startsWith() checks - 'trusted.com' matches 'trusted.com.evil.com'.

high.title: Missing certificate pinning leaves an active TLS bypass unmitigated
high.description:
Two findings in this app combine into a single exploitable path: "No network security config declared" and "WebView ignores TLS certificate errors".

An attacker on the network path - a rogue Wi-Fi access point, a compromised router - presents any certificate and the app accepts it. Nothing else in the app would have caught this: pinning is precisely the mitigation that exists for a bypass like this one.

Attack path:
1. No certificate pinning or network security config is declared (AndroidManifest.xml).
2. WebView ignores TLS certificate errors accepts any certificate at sources/edu/ksu/cs/benign/MyWebViewClient.java:25.
3. An attacker on the network path intercepts and reads or modifies traffic to those endpoints.
high.impact: An attacker on the network path - a rogue Wi-Fi access point, a compromised router - presents any certificate and the app accepts it. Nothing else in the app would have caught this: pinning is precisely the mitigation that exists for a bypass like this one.
high.recommendation: Fix the TLS bypass first - it is the actual defect. Then add certificate pinning (a network security config pin-set, or OkHttp's CertificatePinner) for the app's own endpoints, so a future regression like this one is still caught in transit rather than depending on this code path alone staying correct.

high.title: WebView ignores TLS certificate errors
high.description: onReceivedSslError() calls handler.proceed(), which accepts invalid or untrusted certificates instead of failing the load. The application disables SSL certificate validation by calling handler.proceed() within onReceivedSslError. This allows the app to accept any SSL certificate, including self-signed or invalid ones, making the app vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks.
high.impact: Any attacker on the network path can present their own certificate and read or modify the traffic in this WebView.

high.title: WebView loads a URL taken from an Intent extra
high.description: A WebView load call is fed data that originates from an Intent, so whoever can send that Intent controls what the WebView loads. The application loads a URL in a WebView using a value from an Intent extra ('ssn') concatenated to a base URL. Because WebActivity is exported (AndroidManifest.xml:20), an external application can start this activity and provide a crafted 'ssn' value containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../admin') to force the WebView to load arbitrary paths on the host 10.0.2.2:5000.
high.impact: With a JavaScript bridge or file access enabled on the same WebView, this is the deep-link to WebView chain: attacker content running with the app's bridge privileges.

low.impact: If the WebView is redirected to a malicious site, the application will automatically send the provided credentials to that site.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The android:debuggable attribute is set to true in the AndroidManifest.xml.
info.impact: Enables the use of a debugger, allows access to app data via run-as, and exposes sensitive internal state, significantly lowering the bar for reverse engineering and exploitation.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Confirmed as part of chain-001: Missing certificate pinning leaves an active TLS bypass unmitigated.

info.title: No screenshot protection: FLAG_SECURE is never set
info.description: Nothing in the app sets WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, so every screen can be screenshotted or recorded and appears in the recent-apps snapshot.
info.impact: Credentials, balances or personal data on screen end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview.
info.recommendation: Set FLAG_SECURE on the windows of screens that show credentials or account data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: Private network address 10.0.2.2 shipped in the app
info.description: A private (RFC 1918) address appears in resources/res/values/strings.xml at line 33. It names a development or internal host and grants nothing by itself; it is recorded because it tells a reader about internal infrastructure, or that a development endpoint shipped in the build.

info.recommendation: Point release builds at production hosts through build configuration, and leave development addresses out of them.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets Android API level 27, which permits cleartext (HTTP) traffic by default.
info.impact: Network traffic sent over HTTP is vulnerable to interception and modification via man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.

info.title: WebView loading outside URLs shares the app's cookies
info.description: This WebView loads a URL another app chooses and keeps the app's cookie store, so the page it opens can set cookies the app's own pages then send - overwriting a session cookie with the attacker's, for one.
info.impact: A page an attacker gets loaded plants cookies for the app's web content (cookie tossing or session fixation) or reads the ones its domain can see.
